cases.excerpt: We tested this hypothesis in a prospective case-control study of 476 PCa cases and matched control subjects nested in the Physicians’ Health Study. effect_size.excerpt: Intriguingly, when considering fat and fatty acid sources, we observed a positive association of total fat from dairy with the incidence of PCa (full adjusted HR Q4vs.Q1 : 1.13; 95% CI: 1.02–1.25; P for trend = 0.069), and association similar to PCa incidence was observed between SFAs from dairy intake (full adjusted HR Q4vs.Q1 : 1.12; 95% CI: 1.01–1.25; P for trend = 0.059) in the Table 2 . confidence_interval.excerpt: As Supplementary Table S7 shows, after full adjustment for potential confounders including demographic characteristics and key dietary nutrients (model 3), higher dietary total fat, SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs, and trans-fat acids intake were not associated with the incidence of PCa, with the HRs Q4vs.Q1 (95%CIs) for overall PCa incidence being 1.09 (0.93–1.28), 0.95 (0.82–1.10), 1.03 (0.92–1.15), 1.12 (0.98–1.27), and 0.95 (0.86–1.06), respectively (all P for trend >0.05). sample_size.excerpt: A nested case-control study was conducted among 14,916 apparently healthy men who provided blood samples in 1982. Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

cases.excerpt: Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

effect_size.excerpt: Whole blood levels of all long-chain n-3 fatty acids examined and of linoleic acid were inversely related to overall prostate cancer risk (RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.59; 95% CI, 0.38-0.93; P(trend) = 0.01 for total long-chain n-3 fatty acids and RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.62; 95% CI, 0.41-0.95; P(trend) = 0.03 for linoleic). Blood levels of gamma-linolenic and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acids, fatty acids resulting from the metabolism of linoleic acid, were directly associated with prostate cancer (RR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.94-2.12; P(trend) = 0.05 for gamma-linolenic and RR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.03-2.30; P(trend) = 0.02 for dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Blood levels of gamma-linolenic and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acids, fatty acids resulting from the metabolism of linoleic acid, were directly associated with prostate cancer (RR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.94-2.12; P(trend) = 0.05 for gamma-linolenic and RR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.03-2.30; P(trend) = 0.02 for dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid).

sample_size.excerpt: A nested case-control study was conducted among 14,916 apparently healthy men who provided blood samples in 1982. Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

cases.excerpt: Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

effect_size.excerpt: Whole blood levels of all long-chain n-3 fatty acids examined and of linoleic acid were inversely related to overall prostate cancer risk (RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.59; 95% CI, 0.38-0.93; P(trend) = 0.01 for total long-chain n-3 fatty acids and RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.62; 95% CI, 0.41-0.95; P(trend) = 0.03 for linoleic). Blood levels of gamma-linolenic and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acids, fatty acids resulting from the metabolism of linoleic acid, were directly associated with prostate cancer (RR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.94-2.12; P(trend) = 0.05 for gamma-linolenic and RR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.03-2.30; P(trend) = 0.02 for dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Blood levels of gamma-linolenic and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acids, fatty acids resulting from the metabolism of linoleic acid, were directly associated with prostate cancer (RR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.94-2.12; P(trend) = 0.05 for gamma-linolenic and RR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.03-2.30; P(trend) = 0.02 for dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid).

sample_size.excerpt: A nested case-control study was conducted among 14,916 apparently healthy men who provided blood samples in 1982. Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

cases.excerpt: Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

effect_size.excerpt: Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate the relative risks (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) of total, non-aggressive (stage A/B and Gleason < 7) and aggressive (stage C/D, Gleason >or= 7, subsequent distant metastasis or death) prostate cancer associated with blood levels of specific fatty acids expressed as percentages of total fatty acids. Whole blood levels of all long-chain n-3 fatty acids examined and of linoleic acid were inversely related to overall prostate cancer risk (RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.59; 95% CI, 0.38-0.93; P(trend) = 0.01 for total long-chain n-3 fatty acids and RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.62; 95% CI, 0.41-0.95; P(trend) = 0.03 for linoleic).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Whole blood levels of all long-chain n-3 fatty acids examined and of linoleic acid were inversely related to overall prostate cancer risk (RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.59; 95% CI, 0.38-0.93; P(trend) = 0.01 for total long-chain n-3 fatty acids and RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.62; 95% CI, 0.41-0.95; P(trend) = 0.03 for linoleic).

sample_size.excerpt: A nested case-control study was conducted among 14,916 apparently healthy men who provided blood samples in 1982. Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

cases.excerpt: Blood fatty acid levels were determined for 476 men diagnosed with prostate cancer during a 13-year follow-up and their matched controls.

effect_size.excerpt: Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate the relative risks (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) of total, non-aggressive (stage A/B and Gleason < 7) and aggressive (stage C/D, Gleason >or= 7, subsequent distant metastasis or death) prostate cancer associated with blood levels of specific fatty acids expressed as percentages of total fatty acids. Whole blood levels of all long-chain n-3 fatty acids examined and of linoleic acid were inversely related to overall prostate cancer risk (RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.59; 95% CI, 0.38-0.93; P(trend) = 0.01 for total long-chain n-3 fatty acids and RR(Q5vs.Q1), 0.62; 95% CI, 0.41-0.95; P(trend) = 0.03 for linoleic).

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.1654). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 26 studies yielded an overall effect size of 1.06 (95% CI: 1.01–1.11), suggesting that polyunsaturated fat (pufa) is associated with a higher risk of prostate cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was very high between-study heterogeneity (I² = 81.09%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
